scenes.headline: How OmniRay finds the rays of any lens
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Gnomon! Today: how one model finds where every pixel looks, whatever the lens.

scenes.text: Build the ray field in three rotations on the sphere: a radial base, a smooth correction, then a correction for each pixel.
scenes.say: Build the rays in layers: a simple base, then two corrections that rotate each ray only as far as the lens needs.

scenes.title: Why one curve is not enough

left.title: Lens cameras
left.say: For lens cameras, pixels at the same radius look the same angle off the axis. One rising curve fits.

right.title: A 2:1 panorama
right.say: In a panorama, two pixels at one radius can look opposite ways. No curve of radius can fit that.

steps.say: One image goes into a vision encoder. No camera information.
A small head writes a monotone curve from radius to angle. That is the radial base.
A smooth spherical harmonic correction rotates every ray, from coefficients shared by the whole image.
A last small rotation for each pixel gives a unit ray everywhere.
Point A is nearer the centre than B but looks further off axis. Radius alone cannot order them.
So the corrections rotate rays on the sphere itself.

scenes.label: panorama ray error, radial base to all three stages
scenes.note: our toy fit of the three stages to analytic rays
scenes.say: In my toy fit, the radial base leaves a panorama tens of degrees off. Two residuals bring it under a tenth of a degree.

scenes.label: fisheye example ray error, OmniRay vs UniK3D
scenes.note: from the point clouds on the project page
scenes.say: On the project page's fisheye example, the rays are far closer to the truth. One image, so a spot check.

scenes.text: The lens decides the rays. Build them as a simple base plus residuals, and one model can read any camera.
scenes.say: The lens decides the rays, so build them as a base plus residuals.
